theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Who are the three main parties in industrial relations in Jamaica?
options: Employers, workers and unions, and government
Employers, customers and the company's shareholders
Workers, the news media and the courts of law
Unions, suppliers and the banks that lend to firms

questions.stem: Why should a manufacturing firm in Spanish Town have a written workplace relations policy?
options: So that managers can avoid talking with any union
So that wages can be changed without asking workers
So staff know how issues are raised and handled
So that the firm need not follow the labour relations law

questions.stem: A supervisor at a Kingston factory tells a new worker that joining a union will hurt his chances of promotion. How does this fit with Jamaica's labour relations law?
options: It is allowed, as long as the supervisor says it politely
It goes against the worker's protected right to join a union
It is allowed if the firm does not yet have a union
It is required, so the worker knows the firm's view

questions.stem: A union says it represents most of the line workers at a juice plant in St Catherine and asks the company to bargain with it. The company disagrees. Under Jamaica's labour relations system, how is this usually settled?
options: The company decides alone whether to accept the claim
The union strikes until the company agrees to bargain
The workers' supervisors vote on whether to accept it
A poll of the workers is arranged by the Ministry of Labour

questions.stem: In industrial relations, what is a "bargaining unit"?
options: The room where the union and management hold talks
A team of managers who prepare the firm's wage offer
The group of workers a union is recognised to bargain for
The part of a pay rise that is paid as a lump sum

questions.stem: What is a collective agreement?
options: A written agreement between employer and union on pay and terms
A contract that each worker signs when first hired by the firm
A list of the union's demands sent to management before talks
A decision made by the courts in a workplace dispute

questions.stem: Which item would normally be found in a collective agreement for hotel workers?
options: The hotel's marketing plan for the winter season
Pay rates, hours of work and the grievance procedure
The names and home addresses of the union members
The hotel's room rates and its occupancy targets

questions.stem: What is the main role of a union delegate (shop steward) in the workplace?
options: To manage the department's budget with the supervisor
To decide which workers are dismissed for misconduct
To sign the employer's contracts with its suppliers
To represent members and raise their concerns with managers

questions.stem: A worker at a bauxite company feels she was unfairly passed over for overtime. What should she use first?
options: The company's grievance procedure
A complaint to the Industrial Disputes Tribunal
A strike called by her own work group
A letter to the newspaper about the company

questions.stem: A supervisor receives a formal grievance from a worker about unfair treatment. What should she do first?
options: Tell the worker it will be looked at after the busy season
Discuss the grievance with the worker's friends in the canteen
Meet the worker promptly, as the procedure says
Pass the grievance straight to the company's lawyers

questions.stem: Why do most grievance procedures set a time limit for each stage?
options: So managers can delay matters for as long as they need
So workers lose the right to complain after one week
So that only urgent problems are heard by managers
So that problems are dealt with before they grow

questions.stem: A security officer at a Montego Bay hotel is accused of sleeping on duty. Which step is essential before any disciplinary decision is made?
options: Telling the other officers the outcome before the hearing
Telling him the allegation and letting him answer it
Asking him to resign quietly so that no record is kept
Cutting his pay at once while the matter is looked at

questions.stem: At a disciplinary hearing, a worker asks to bring his union delegate. What should the manager do?
options: Refuse, since the hearing is a private matter for the firm
Agree only if the delegate promises not to speak at all
Agree, as fair procedure lets the worker be represented
Postpone the hearing until the worker drops the request

questions.stem: Two cashiers at a supermarket chain broke the same cash-handling rule. One received a warning and the other was dismissed. What is the main problem?
options: Unequal treatment, which makes the dismissal look unfair
The warning was too harsh for a first breach of the rule
Both cashiers should have been dismissed on the same day
There is none, as managers may choose freely each time

questions.stem: A manager hears that a forklift driver used his phone while driving in the warehouse. What should he do before holding a disciplinary hearing?
options: Dismiss the driver at once to show that safety matters
Investigate, collecting statements and footage
Ask the driver's union to decide what action to take
Wait to see whether the driver does it a second time

questions.stem: A dispute about a worker's dismissal has been referred to the Industrial Disputes Tribunal. What should the employer prepare?
options: A statement that it will not attend the hearing
Only the worker's original application form
A letter asking that the union be kept out of the case
Records showing the reasons and the fair process followed

questions.stem: What does the Ministry of Labour's conciliation service do in a workplace dispute?
options: It decides which side is right and fines the side at fault
It runs the company until the dispute has been settled
It helps the two sides talk and reach their own agreement
It represents the workers against the employer in court

questions.stem: Talks between the union and management at a cement plant have failed to settle a wage dispute. What is usually the next step?
options: Ask the Ministry of Labour to help through conciliation
Take the dispute straight to the Court of Appeal
Lock the workers out until they accept the offer
Replace the union with one the company prefers

questions.stem: The Industrial Disputes Tribunal makes an award in a dispute between a hotel and its workers' union. What is the general effect of the award?
options: It is advice that either side may choose to ignore
It applies only if the workers vote to accept it
It lasts only until the next general election
It is binding on the employer and the workers

questions.stem: Workers at a port refuse to do anything beyond the exact wording of their job descriptions, which slows the work. What is this called?
options: A lockout
A work-to-rule
A sit-down strike
A lay-off

questions.stem: During a pay dispute, many nurses at a hospital call in sick on the same day. What is this kind of industrial action usually called?
options: A lockout
A go-slow
A sick-out
A picket line

questions.stem: Workers at a manufacturing plant have stopped work in a dispute. What should management do first?
options: Stay calm and keep talking with the union
Dismiss all the workers who stopped work that morning
Speak to the media and blame the union for the stoppage
Cut off contact with the union until the workers return

questions.stem: A company has 120 workers paid an average of J$80,000 a month. The union asks for a 6% increase. What would the increase cost the company in a year?
A two-year agreement gives 5% in the first year and 4% in the second, each on the pay at the time. A worker now earns J$100,000 a month. What will she earn a month in the second year?
A bottling plant makes 2,000 cases a day, and each case earns a contribution of J$1,500. How much contribution is lost if a stoppage lasts three days?
Before wage talks begin, what should the company's negotiating team agree with the board?
options: The names of the union members who will attend the talks
A promise that the first offer will never be changed
Its mandate: the highest offer and terms it may agree
A press statement saying that the talks have failed

questions.stem: In wage talks at a hotel, the union insists on a 12% increase. By asking questions, the manager learns that workers mainly worry about travel costs on late shifts. What should the manager explore?
options: Refusing any increase until the union drops its demand
Late-shift transport or an allowance, with a smaller rise
Giving all the late shifts to workers who live nearby
Offering the full 12% at once to end the talks quickly

questions.stem: Which behaviour in collective bargaining shows good faith?
options: Refusing to share any figures about the firm's finances
Making a final offer at the first meeting and walking out
Agreeing terms in talks, then changing them in writing
Meeting often, sharing facts, seeking agreement

questions.stem: Management and the union reach agreement late at night after long talks. What should happen before they leave the room?
options: Each side should give the media its own version
The manager should email the workers with the news
The main terms should be written and signed
Nothing, as the lawyers can write it up next month

questions.stem: After a new collective agreement is signed, what should the human resource manager do?
options: Brief supervisors and update payroll, policies and records
File it away until the next round of talks in two years
Leave it to the union to tell the supervisors about it
Give copies of the agreement to senior managers only

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a joint consultative committee of managers and worker representatives?
options: To negotiate each worker's own pay increase
To discuss workplace issues and plans before decisions
To hear appeals against dismissal instead of the Tribunal
To decide the company's prices and marketing plans

questions.stem: Which sign most suggests that workplace relations in a department are getting worse?
options: More workers asking about training courses
A rise in the number of job applications
Staff taking their annual leave as planned
Rising absence, grievances and turnover

questions.stem: A company must cut 30 posts because a major contract has ended. Which approach fits fair practice and the general purpose of the law on redundancy?
options: Consult early, use fair selection criteria and pay what is due
Choose the workers who complain most and give a day's notice
Call the dismissals misconduct so that nothing has to be paid
Tell the workers on payday, without telling the union first

questions.stem: Which step could reduce the need for redundancies when work falls?
options: Hiring new staff on lower pay to replace current workers
Raising the overtime worked by the remaining workers
Freezing hiring, cutting overtime and redeploying staff
Asking workers to resign without any redundancy pay

questions.stem: A firm wants to change its workers' hours from a five-day to a six-day week. What should management do?
options: Post the new hours on the notice board and start next week
Consult the workers and their union and seek agreement first
Dismiss any worker who will not accept the new hours that day
Change the hours only for the workers who are not in the union

questions.stem: A manager suggests not renewing a worker's contract because she is pregnant. What should the human resource manager advise?
options: Agree, as long as the reason is never written down
Agree, if she has been with the firm less than two years
Delay the decision until after the baby is born
Refuse, as it is unfair and may break employment law

questions.stem: Workers at a factory refuse to use a machine they believe is unsafe, and the union backs them. What should the manager do first?
options: Order them back to the machine or face discipline
Ask other workers to use the machine in their place
Stop the machine and have it checked with the workers
Tell the union that safety is not a matter for it

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the line manager's role in workplace relations?
options: Handling daily issues fairly before they grow
Leaving all union matters to the human resource department
Making sure the union has no contact with front-line staff
Setting the pay rates for the whole organisation each year

questions.stem: Why should a manager keep careful records of grievance and disciplinary meetings?
options: So the records can be shared with other firms when hiring
So that workers can be reminded of their mistakes each year
So the manager need not follow the written procedure
They show a fair process was followed if it is challenged

questions.stem: A supervisor wants to tell the team why a colleague was given a final warning. What is the correct approach?
options: Tell the team, so everyone learns from the colleague's mistake
Keep the details confidential to those who need to know
Post a short summary of the warning on the notice board
Ask the colleague to explain the warning to the team himself

questions.stem: A union delegate asks to meet the plant manager about rumours of a new shift system. The plans are still being drawn up. What is the best response?
options: Deny that any changes are being considered at all
Refuse to meet until the plans have been finalised
Meet, share what can be shared and promise consultation
Give the delegate the full plans before the board sees them

questions.stem: In a dispute, an employer closes the workplace and keeps the workers out until they accept its terms. What is this called?
options: A lockout
A work-to-rule
A go-slow
A sympathy strike

questions.stem: When preparing for wage talks, why does a company look at pay for similar jobs at other firms in the area?
options: To find workers it can hire away from its competitors
So it can pay less than every other firm in the parish
To prove to the union that its claim is always too high
To judge whether its own offer is fair and competitive

questions.stem: Which is NOT a usual stage in a workplace grievance procedure?
options: Raising the matter with the immediate supervisor
Posting the complaint on the company's social media
Taking it to a more senior manager if not settled
A final appeal to a senior manager or a panel

questions.stem: Which practice does most to build trust between management and the workforce over time?
options: Keeping promises and sharing information openly
Giving a bonus only when the union threatens action
Meeting the union only when there is a crisis
Making changes quickly before workers find out

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Give the full name or the initials of the Jamaican tribunal that hears industrial disputes referred to it and makes binding awards.
Which government ministry offers conciliation to help employers and unions settle disputes?
accepted: Ministry of Labour and Social Security
the Ministry of Labour and Social Security

shortAnswers.stem: What term describes talks between an employer and a union to agree pay and conditions for a group of workers?
What is the name of the written process a worker uses to raise a complaint about their treatment at work?
A union asks for a 10% increase and management offers 4%. If they settle exactly halfway, what increase is agreed?
A company's monthly payroll is J$5,000,000. How much more will it cost each month if all pay rises by 3%? Give the answer in J$.
What term is used for the principles of fair procedure, such as the right to know the case against you and to answer it before an unbiased person?
What term describes workers standing outside a workplace during a dispute to make their case and persuade others not to go in?
What term describes workers deliberately working more slowly than normal as a form of industrial action?
What one word names the ending of a worker's job because the work has ended or reduced, not because of the worker's conduct?
A company's grievance log shows that 18 of 24 grievances were settled at the first stage. What percentage is this?
What term describes a worker resigning because the employer's serious breach of the contract left them no real choice?
A union represents 270 of the 450 workers in a bargaining unit. What percentage of the workers is this?
What term describes a stoppage by workers in support of another group's dispute rather than their own?
After a fair hearing, what document tells a worker that one more breach of the rules may lead to dismissal?

essays.stem: The workers at a 200-room resort in Ocho Rios have recently voted to be represented by a union. As the new human resource manager, plan how you would build good working relations with the union and the staff in the first year.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by meeting the union's officers and delegates early to show that management accepts the result and wants a constructive relationship. Together we would agree how we will work: who meets, how often, and how issues are raised. I would brief all managers and supervisors on the workers' rights under Jamaica's labour relations law, the duty to bargain in good faith and the need to treat union members fairly, with training in handling grievances and discipline. I would review the grievance and disciplinary procedures with the union so they are clear, fair and have time limits. Before the first round of collective bargaining, I would gather pay data, cost possible claims and agree a mandate with the board. I would set up a joint consultative committee to discuss issues such as rosters, safety and seasonal staffing before decisions are made. I would keep staff informed through briefings and the notice board. Throughout the year I would track absence, grievances, turnover and survey results to see whether relations are improving.
markingPoints: Accepts the result and meets the union early to agree how to work together
Trains managers and supervisors on rights, fair treatment and procedures
Reviews grievance and disciplinary procedures jointly
Prepares for bargaining and sets up consultation
Communicates with staff and monitors indicators of relations

essays.stem: Describe the stages a Jamaican employer and union would usually go through to settle a pay dispute, from talks at the workplace to the Industrial Disputes Tribunal, and explain the purpose of each stage.
essays.modelAnswer: The first stage is direct talks between management and the union at the workplace, following any procedure in the collective agreement. The purpose is for the two sides, who know the business best, to reach their own agreement, and most disputes are settled here. If talks break down, either side can ask the Ministry of Labour for help. The Ministry's conciliation officers meet the two sides, together and apart, to clarify the issues, test the positions and suggest ways forward. Conciliation does not impose a decision; its purpose is to help the parties find an agreement they both accept. If conciliation fails, the dispute may be referred to the Industrial Disputes Tribunal, as the labour relations law provides. The Tribunal hears evidence and arguments from both sides and makes an award, which is binding on them. Its purpose is to give a final, independent settlement so that a long dispute does not continue to harm the business and the workers. Throughout, both sides should keep records and avoid action that makes the dispute worse.
markingPoints: Direct workplace talks first, under the agreed procedure
Conciliation by the Ministry of Labour, which helps but does not decide
Referral to the Industrial Disputes Tribunal if conciliation fails
The Tribunal hears both sides and makes a binding award
Explains the purpose of each stage

essays.stem: The 200 workers in a company's bargaining unit earn an average of J$90,000 a month. The union claims an 8% increase. The board will allow no more than J$9,720,000 extra a year. Work out what the claim would cost in a year and the largest percentage increase the board's limit allows, then explain how you would prepare the company's team for the talks.
essays.modelAnswer: An 8% increase is J$7,200 a month per worker. For 200 workers that is J$1,440,000 a month, or J$17,280,000 a year. The board's limit of J$9,720,000 a year is J$810,000 a month, or J$4,050 per worker, which is 4.5% of J$90,000. So the gap between the claim and the mandate is 3.5 percentage points. To prepare, I would confirm the mandate in writing with the board, including whether other items, such as allowances, count against the limit. I would gather facts: the company's financial position, pay for similar jobs in the area, inflation, productivity and absence. I would study the union's claim to understand the workers' main concerns and look for low-cost options, such as transport or shift changes, that meet real interests. I would plan an opening offer below 4.5% so there is room to move, and list possible trade-offs. The team would agree roles: a lead speaker, a note-taker and someone to check the costings. We would agree to keep a respectful tone and to put any settlement in writing.
markingPoints: Works out the claim correctly: J$1,440,000 a month, J$17,280,000 a year
Works out the mandate correctly: J$4,050 per worker, 4.5%
Confirms the mandate and gathers relevant facts
Looks for the workers' underlying interests and possible trade-offs
Plans opening offer, team roles and recording the agreement

essays.stem: A supermarket manager suspects that a stock clerk has been taking goods without paying. Describe a fair disciplinary procedure for the case, and explain why each step matters.
essays.modelAnswer: First the manager should investigate before making any decision. This means checking stock records and camera footage and taking written statements from witnesses. It matters because a decision must rest on evidence, not suspicion. If the case is serious, the clerk may be suspended on full pay while the investigation is done, so that evidence is protected without punishing him in advance. Next, the clerk should be told in writing what he is accused of and given the evidence, with reasonable notice of a hearing. He should be told he may bring a union delegate or a colleague. This lets him prepare a proper answer. At the hearing, which should be led by a manager who was not involved in the investigation, the clerk is allowed to explain and challenge the evidence. This follows natural justice and reduces bias. The manager should then decide fairly, considering his record and how similar cases were treated, and give the decision in writing with the right of appeal. Finally, everything should be recorded and kept confidential, because records show the process was fair if the dismissal is challenged.
markingPoints: Investigates and gathers evidence before deciding
Uses suspension on pay only where needed, not as a punishment
Informs the worker in writing and allows representation
Holds a fair hearing with an unbiased manager and lets the worker answer
Decides consistently, gives the right of appeal and keeps confidential records

essays.stem: At a call centre in Montego Bay, absence, grievances and staff turnover have all risen over the last six months. Analyse the likely causes and recommend actions to improve workplace relations.
essays.modelAnswer: Rising absence, grievances and turnover together suggest a problem with how staff feel they are treated, rather than one isolated issue. Likely causes include heavy workloads and tight call targets, rosters changed at short notice, supervisors who handle problems poorly, pay that has fallen behind other call centres, or poor communication about changes. To find the real causes, I would analyse the grievance log for common themes, look at exit interview notes and absence patterns by team and supervisor, and run a short anonymous staff survey. I would also meet the union or staff representatives. Based on the findings, actions might include training supervisors in fair, consistent handling of issues, publishing rosters earlier, reviewing call targets with staff, and checking pay against the market. I would set up regular consultation meetings so concerns are heard early, and give quick feedback on what has been done. I would set targets, for example to reduce absence and turnover over six months, track them monthly and report progress to staff.
markingPoints: Recognises the indicators point to a wider relations problem
Suggests plausible causes (workload, rosters, supervision, pay, communication)
Uses evidence to confirm the causes (grievance log, exit interviews, survey, union views)
Recommends practical actions matched to the causes
Sets targets, consults and monitors progress

essays.stem: Workers at a manufacturing plant in May Pen have begun a sick-out because an agreed pay increase is late. Explain how management should respond in the first week.
essays.modelAnswer: Management should first stay calm and avoid threats, because a hasty reaction can turn a short protest into a long dispute. The plant manager should find out the facts: why the increase is late, how many workers are involved and what effect it is having on production and customers. Since the cause is a broken commitment, management should contact the union at once, admit the delay, explain the reason honestly and give a firm date for payment if possible. A meeting with the union should be held within a day or two to agree a way forward, such as paying the increase with back pay by a set date. If talks do not settle it, management can ask the Ministry of Labour for conciliation. Meanwhile, management should keep essential work and safety covered, tell key customers about possible delays, and brief supervisors to treat workers respectfully. Sick leave rules should be applied fairly and consistently. Once the matter is settled, management should review why the payment was late and fix the cause so trust is rebuilt.
markingPoints: Stays calm and avoids threats or hasty discipline
Finds the facts and the effect of the action
Contacts the union quickly, admits the delay and offers a firm solution
Uses conciliation if talks fail, while protecting safety and customers
Reviews the cause afterwards to rebuild trust

essays.stem: A distribution company in Kingston must cut 30 of its 150 posts after losing a major contract. Explain how the company should manage the redundancies fairly and in line with the general purpose of the law.
essays.modelAnswer: The company should first confirm the business reason and look at ways to reduce job losses, such as freezing hiring, cutting overtime, ending temporary contracts and moving staff to other work. It should consult the union and the affected workers early, before decisions are final, explaining the reasons, the number of posts and the proposed selection method, and listening to their ideas. Selection must use fair, objective criteria agreed in advance, such as skills, performance records and length of service, and must not be based on union membership, pregnancy, or other unfair grounds. Each affected worker should be told in a private meeting, with a letter setting out the reason, their notice, the redundancy payment due under the law and their employment contract, and any right of appeal. The company should offer support, such as time off to look for work, references and help with job searches. It should keep careful records of the process. Finally, it should look after the remaining staff, who may be worried, by explaining the company's plans and how work will be reorganised.
markingPoints: Looks for alternatives to reduce job losses
Consults the union and workers early
Uses fair, objective, agreed selection criteria and avoids unfair grounds
Tells workers privately and in writing, with notice and payments due
Supports those leaving, keeps records and looks after those who stay

essays.stem: Compare a cooperative approach to industrial relations with an adversarial one, and recommend which a company should aim for, with reasons.
essays.modelAnswer: In an adversarial approach, management and the union see each other as opponents. Each side hides information, makes extreme opening demands and tries to win at the other's expense. Disputes are frequent and are often settled only by conciliation, the Tribunal or industrial action. This approach may bring short-term gains for one side, but it damages trust, raises the risk of stoppages and makes change slow and costly. In a cooperative approach, the two sides accept that they have different interests but also shared ones, such as the survival of the business and good jobs. They share information, consult before decisions, solve problems jointly and bargain in good faith. Disputes still happen, but more are settled early at the workplace. This approach takes time and needs managers and union leaders who keep their word. I would recommend that a company aim for a cooperative approach, because it supports productivity, makes change easier and lowers the cost of disputes. It does not mean giving in; management still sets a clear mandate and protects the business.
markingPoints: Describes the adversarial approach and its effects
Describes the cooperative approach and its features
Compares costs and benefits of each
Makes a clear recommendation
Justifies it, noting that cooperation still needs firm, fair management

essays.stem: Design a three-stage grievance procedure for a medium-sized company, and explain how managers should handle grievances under it.
essays.modelAnswer: Stage one: the worker raises the grievance with the immediate supervisor, by speaking or in writing. The supervisor meets the worker within three working days, listens, checks the facts and gives an answer within five working days. Stage two: if the worker is not satisfied, they put the grievance in writing to the department manager, who meets them within five working days and replies in writing within a further five. Stage three: if it is still not settled, the worker appeals to a senior manager or panel not involved earlier, whose written decision ends the internal process. At each stage the worker may bring a union delegate or colleague. If the grievance concerns the supervisor, the worker can start at stage two. Managers should treat every grievance seriously and promptly, listen without becoming defensive, investigate fairly, keep the matter confidential and make sure no worker is punished for raising a grievance. They should record each meeting and decision. Managers should also look at grievance trends, because repeated complaints may show a wider problem that needs fixing.
markingPoints: Sets three clear stages with rising levels of management
Includes time limits and written replies
Allows representation and a route that avoids the person complained about
Explains fair handling: prompt, listening, investigating, no victimisation
Keeps records and reviews trends

essays.stem: A union writes to a courier company saying it represents most of the company's 80 drivers and asks for bargaining rights. Explain how the company should respond, and how such a claim is usually decided in Jamaica.
essays.modelAnswer: The company should respond politely and promptly in writing, acknowledging the letter. It should not ignore the claim or react against the drivers, because Jamaica's labour relations law protects workers' right to join a union and to take part in its activities, and any threat or punishment for joining would be unlawful and damage relations. Management should brief supervisors not to question drivers about membership or make promises or threats. The company may meet the union to discuss the claim and the group of workers it covers. If the company accepts that the union has majority support, it can recognise the union and begin bargaining. If the company doubts the claim, the usual route is for the matter to go to the Ministry of Labour, which can arrange a poll of the workers to find out whether a majority want the union to represent them. If the union wins the poll, the company is expected to recognise and bargain with it in good faith. Whatever the result, the company should keep communicating with the drivers and treat them fairly.
markingPoints: Responds promptly and politely in writing
Respects the workers' protected right to join a union and avoids threats or questioning
Briefs supervisors on how to behave
Explains the poll arranged through the Ministry of Labour where the claim is disputed
Recognises and bargains in good faith if the union has majority support

practical1.title: Negotiate and record a wage agreement
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case: a food processing company in St Catherine, its bargaining unit of workers, their average pay, the union's claim, the company's financial position and the board's limit for extra pay costs. Your group splits into two sides. Management side (two members): the lead negotiator, who opens and leads the talks, and the costing officer, who works out on a spreadsheet the cost of the claim, the mandate and every offer made, checking each figure twice. Union side (two members): the union officer, who presents the claim, and the union delegate, who speaks for the workers' concerns. The fifth member is the recorder, who keeps notes of every offer and counter-offer and writes up the heads of agreement; in a group of four, the costing officer also keeps the record. Before the talks, each side spends 40 minutes preparing a written plan (aims, opening position, limit, possible trade-offs). The talks then last up to 45 minutes. If you agree, the recorder writes the heads of agreement and both lead speakers sign it; if you do not, write a note of the issues to be taken to conciliation. Each side then writes a half-page review of what went well and what it would change.
materials: Case pack and confidential briefs for each side from the assessor
Two separate tables for preparation and one table for the talks
Templates for the negotiation plan, notes and heads of agreement
photos: The costing spreadsheet on screen showing the claim, the mandate and each offer
The talks in progress (faces only if all agree)
The recorder's notes of offers and counter-offers
The signed heads of agreement, or the note of issues for conciliation
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Prepared a plan with aims, opening position, limit and trade-offs
Costings of the claim, the mandate and each offer are correct and were checked twice
Negotiated in good faith: listened, asked about interests and stayed respectful
The management side did not go beyond the board's mandate
The agreement or issues note is clear, accurate and complete
Wrote a fair review of their side's performance
safety: Keep each side's confidential brief private until the talks end, then return all papers to the assessor
Use only the made-up case; do not discuss real employers, unions or disputes
Keep the talks respectful: challenge positions, not people
Take a short break between preparation and the talks

practical2.title: Investigate a workplace complaint, hold a fair hearing and write the outcome
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case from a hotel or a factory: a worker is accused of a breach of the rules (for example repeated lateness and leaving a post unattended) and has also raised a grievance that her supervisor treats her unfairly. Each member has a named role: investigating officer (reads the evidence pack, interviews witnesses played by other members, and writes a one-page investigation report); hearing manager (plans and chairs the hearing, then decides and writes the outcome letter with the reasons and the right of appeal); worker (plays the role card from the assessor and answers the allegation); union delegate (supports the worker, asks questions and raises the grievance); note-taker (keeps a full, factual record of the hearing). In a group of four, the investigating officer also takes notes. After the hearing, the group together draws a flowchart of the company's grievance and disciplinary procedures, showing each stage, time limits and the route to conciliation through the Ministry of Labour and, if needed, the Industrial Disputes Tribunal.
materials: Case pack, evidence pack and role cards from the assessor
A room set up for a hearing
Templates for the investigation report, hearing notes and outcome letter
Computer and printer, or paper and pens
photos: The hearing in progress, showing the set-up (faces only if all agree)
The note-taker's record of the hearing
The outcome letter with reasons and right of appeal
The procedure flowchart on the flipchart
checklist: Investigation report sets out facts and evidence fairly before any decision
Worker was told the allegation, shown the evidence and given a chance to answer
Union delegate was allowed to take part and the grievance was heard
Hearing manager stayed impartial, calm and respectful
Outcome is reasonable, consistent and explained in writing with the right of appeal
Hearing notes are accurate and factual
Flowchart shows the stages, time limits and the routes to conciliation and the Tribunal correctly
safety: Use only the made-up case; do not discuss real workers or real disciplinary matters
Keep all notes and letters confidential to the group and the assessor
Keep the role play respectful, and stop if anyone becomes uncomfortable
Photograph faces only if every person agrees and the Centre allows it
